Glossary

Extension or plugin: what is it on a website?

An extension, also called a plugin, is an add-on you plug into a site to teach it to do something new. It is like adding an attachment to a food processor.

The definition in one sentence

The CMS provides the base: pages, menus, accounts. Extensions add the rest: a contact form, a booking module, a photo gallery, a spam filter, a shopping basket.

They are written by thousands of different developers. Some are free, others paid, some are closely maintained, others abandoned for years.

What it does for a small business

Thanks to extensions, a site can grow with your business. You start with a simple presentation, then add online booking when your diary fills up, or online sales the day you launch a product.

A real-life example

An osteopath installs an extension for appointments, one for a gallery, one for reviews, one for speed, one for SEO, and so on. After a year, he has twenty-five. An update to one clashes with another, and the form stops working for a week. He only notices when the requests dry up.

What you need to know

  • Every extension is a door. A badly written or outdated extension is one of the main causes of hacking.
  • Every extension has a weight. It adds code to load, and the site slows down.
  • Updates are essential, but you need to check afterwards that everything still works.
  • An extension can disappear. If its author stops, it no longer gets fixes and has to be replaced.

Before adding one, ask yourself: will I really use it every month? If the answer is no, move on.

Good habits

  • Go for extensions that are well known, recent and well rated.
  • Delete the ones you no longer use, instead of just deactivating them.
  • Make a backup before every major update.

Your questions

How many extensions should a site have?

There is no right number. The rule is simple: only the ones you need, each chosen with care. A small, well-built site often has few.

Are free extensions dangerous?

Not necessarily. Many are excellent and maintained by serious teams. The danger mostly comes from extensions that are no longer updated, free or paid.
